entry.title: Biomechanical Correlates of Soccer-Related Lower-Extremity Injury Vulnerability with Foot-Ankle and Footwear-Surface Implications: Biomechanical Correlates of Soccer Injury Vulnerability.
entry.content:
Luo W, Pan M, Dong Z, Wang Y, et al. · J Am Podiatr Med Assoc · 2026

Background: Soccer places repeated high-intensity mechanical demands on the lower extremities, and lower-limb injuries contribute substantially to the overall injury burden. This systematic review synthesised contemporary evidence on mechanism-relevant biomechanical correlates of lower-extremity injury vulnerability in soccer, including intrinsic neuromuscular/biomechanical characteristics and extrinsic boundary conditions that were examined in relation to injury endpoints and/or injury-mechanism-relevant surrogate outcomes. Methods: Electronic searches of PubMed, Web of Science, Google Scholar, and the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ) were conducted for studies published between 1 January 2021 and 1 April 2026 using Boolean combinations of terms related to soccer/football, lower-extremity injury, and biomechanics/neuromuscular control. PubMed and Web of Science were used as the primary databases, while Google Scholar and DOAJ served as supplementary sources. No language restrictions were applied. Records were managed in Mendeley (v2.144.0), and methodological quality was appraised using the Modified Downs and Black Checklist. Twenty studies met the inclusion criteria and were included in the qualitative synthesis. Results: Lower-extremity injury vulnerability appeared to reflect multiple interacting intrinsic and extrinsic factors under soccer-specific exposure. Intrinsic correlates most frequently examined included neuromuscular control and motor coordination, fatigue-related declines in performance and movement execution, and previous injury/ACLR status, with task-specific alterations reported in cutting, landing, sprinting, and kicking mechanics and/or strength/asymmetry indices. Sex-related differences were also reported. Extrinsic boundary conditions included footwear and playing-surface properties, particularly stiffness and traction, which may influence foot-ground interaction, ankle loading, and ankle-knee mechanical coupling, as well as positional demands associated with different exposure profiles. Conclusions: Overall, the evidence supports an integrated approach to injury-vulnerability management that combines neuromuscular training, fatigue/load monitoring, and context-specific consideration of footwear-surface conditions, with particular relevance to foot-ankle stability and load transmission during soccer-specific movements. However, most included studies quantified surrogate outcomes rather than prospective injury incidence, and inferences should be interpreted accordingly.

entry.title: Rehabilitation after surgery for chronic lateral ankle instability is still a journey in progress: A scoping review.
entry.content:
Erekdag A, Spennacchio P, Prill R, Guelfi M, et al. · J Exp Orthop · 2026

To map the postoperative rehabilitation strategies reported after anatomical lateral ankle stabilisation surgery for chronic lateral ankle instability, with emphasis on immobilizüation, weight-bearing (WB) progression, range of motion, strengthening, neuromuscular rehabilitation and technique-related trends. PubMed (MEDLINE), Embase and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched from 1 January 2010 to 10 September 2025. Original studies including patients aged 16 years or older who underwent anatomical lateral ankle stabilisation procedures and reported postoperative rehabilitation details were eligible. Data were extracted independently by two reviewers and synthesised descriptively using thematic and conceptual mapping. Forty-nine studies involving 2851 participants were included. The pooled mean age was 33.0 ± 11.8 years, and 53.2% of participants were male. Rehabilitation protocols demonstrated substantial heterogeneity across all domains. Immobilization ranged from immediate functional bracing to rigid immobilization for up to 6 weeks. WB progression varied from immediate protected loading to delayed loading, with full WB most commonly achieved between 6 and 8 weeks. Range-of-motion exercises were initiated between the first postoperative day and 4-6 weeks; sagittal-plane motion was generally introduced earlier, whereas inversion and varus stress were more consistently restricted during the early healing. Technique-related patterns suggested earlier functional progression after augmented or functionally braced repairs and more cautious progression after reconstruction or combined procedures. Postoperative rehabilitation after anatomical lateral ankle stabilisation remains highly heterogeneous, and does not support a single universal protocol. The available evidence map supports a staged, biology-informed approach that protects the repair from early inversion and varus stress, restores sagittal-plane motion and gait progressively and advances strengthening and neuromuscular training according to clinical criteria. Prospective comparative studies with standardised rehabilitation reporting are required to establish technique-specific and criterion-based pathways. Level I.

entry.title: Bilateral gait biomechanics in individuals with varying levels of kinesiophobia after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: a cross-sectional study.
entry.content:
Tu J, Li M, Sun Z, Xiu Y, et al. · J Orthop Surg Res · 2026

To investigate whether bilateral gait biomechanical characteristics differ among individuals with varying levels of kinesiophobia after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) and healthy controls. This cross-sectional observational study included 36 individuals who were ≥ 12 months post-ACLR and 18 healthy controls. Individuals after ACLR were classified into high- and low-kinesiophobia groups using a predefined TSK-17 cutoff score of 40. A three-dimensional motion capture system synchronized with force platforms was used to quantify bilateral gait biomechanics during self-selected walking, including spatiotemporal, kinematic, and kinetic parameters. Limb symmetry indices (LSIs) were calculated for prespecified bilateral gait variables, and exploratory analyses examined associations between continuous TSK-17 scores and biomechanical outcomes. Compared with healthy controls, individuals after ACLR demonstrated reduced knee flexion-extension range of motion (ROM), with greater reductions in the high-kinesiophobia group than in the low-kinesiophobia group. Specifically, the involved limb had a 10.0° lower knee flexion-extension ROM in the high-kinesiophobia group than in the low-kinesiophobia group (95% CI 5.8-14.2°). The contralateral limb also showed reduced knee flexion-extension ROM compared with healthy controls in both ACLR groups (high-kinesiophobia group: mean difference - 7.3°, 95% CI - 10.7 to - 3.9°; low-kinesiophobia group: mean difference - 6.4°, 95% CI - 9.8 to - 3.0°). Differences in selected joint moments, including hip adduction, knee varus-valgus, and ankle inversion-eversion moments, were joint- and limb-specific among groups. Knee flexion-extension ROM LSI differed among groups, with greater deviations from 100% observed in both ACLR groups than in healthy controls, indicating differences in numerical bilateral symmetry estimates. Exploratory analyses identified no consistent associations between continuous TSK-17 scores and gait biomechanical variables after correction for multiple comparisons. Varying levels of kinesiophobia after ACLR were associated with differences in bilateral gait biomechanics, particularly knee flexion-extension ROM. TSK-17 scores alone may not be sufficient to identify individual gait abnormalities; therefore, integrating psychological assessment with objective gait evaluation may provide a more comprehensive basis for individualized rehabilitation planning.

entry.title: Impacts of emotional priming during multiple object tracking tasks on drop landing strategy in individuals with functional ankle instability: an exploratory study.
entry.content:
Xue J, Kong L, Zhou Z, Han X, et al. · J Neuroeng Rehabil · 2026

Attentional resources play a critical role in voluntary movement execution under dual-task (DT) conditions, such as Multiple Object Tracking (MOT). Efficient resource allocation requires cognitive adjustments, which may divert attention from motor control and exacerbate movement deficits. Functional Ankle Instability (FAI) is characterized by impaired proprioception, neuromuscular dysfunction and compromised motor strategy, often resulting in inefficient landing strategies. While emotional priming has been shown to influence cognitive and motor performance, its specific impact on drop landing strategies in FAI individuals during cognitively demanding tasks remains unclear. This study aims to examine how different emotional priming conditions influence the biomechanical characteristics of drop landing strategies in individuals with FAI while performing an MOT task. Fourteen individuals with FAI and fourteen matched healthy controls participated in a drop landing experiment under dual-task (MOT) and single-task conditions. Three emotional states-Neutral Emotion (NEm), Negative Emotion (NEg), and Positive Emotion (PE)-were induced through priming. Kinematic and kinetic data were collected using a Vicon motion capture system and a Kistler force plate. A 2 × 2 × 3 mixed-design ANOVA was conducted to assess the effects of group, task conditions, and emotional state. Significant interaction effects between task condition and group were observed, especially in hip flexion at Initial Contact (IC) and knee stiffness. Under DT conditions, individuals with FAI demonstrated reduced hip flexion (p = 0.001) and increased knee stiffness (p = 0.004), indicating a rigid landing pattern. Emotional priming interacted with task condition to modulate joint kinematics and kinetics. Specifically, under DT conditions, PE enhanced ankle plantarflexion (p = 0.002) and reduced knee flexion at IC (p = 0.018), while NEm reduced hip flexion at peak Vertical Ground Reaction Force (VGRF) (p = 0.016) and increased hip stiffness (p = 0.044). In particular, following a significant three-way interaction, simple-simple effect analyses revealed that for individuals with FAI under dual-task landing, peak VGRF in the NEm condition was significantly higher than in the PE condition (p = 0.038). Under the same dual-task condition, lower extremity stiffness in the NEm condition differed significantly from both the PE (p = 0.033) and NEg (p = 0.022) conditions, while hip energy absorption in the NEm condition differed significantly only from the NEg condition (p = 0.038). Additionally, within the NEm condition, hip energy absorption was significantly greater during dual-task landing than during single-task landing (p = 0.039). Dual-tasking elicits a more rigid landing strategy in individuals with FAI, marked by elevated knee stiffness and reduced hip flexion. Emotional priming further modulates these dual-task-related biomechanical alterations. Compared with the NEm condition, both PE and NEg conditions attenuated selected indicators of landing rigidity; the PE condition additionally decreased peak VGRF, whereas the NEg condition reduced hip energy absorption. These effects appeared to occur through distinct biomechanical pathways, with PE primarily influencing impact loading and NEg influencing proximal mechanical contribution. These findings provide preliminary evidence that emotional modulation may influence landing biomechanics under cognitive load and may have implications for injury prevention strategies in individuals with FAI.

entry.title: Association Between Dynamic Tibiotalar Motion and Patient-Reported Outcomes After Total Ankle Arthroplasty With a Total Talar Prosthesis.
entry.content:
Kurokawa H, Ikeda R, Kosugi S, Yamamoto M, et al. · Foot Ankle Orthop · 2026

Although numerous studies have investigated the influence of preoperative deformity and postoperative implant alignment on clinical outcomes after total ankle arthroplasty (TAA), the relationship between dynamic tibiotalar motion and patient-reported outcomes remains unclear. This pilot study investigated whether preoperative, postoperative, and longitudinal changes in computed tomography (CT)-based tibiotalar kinematics are associated with clinical outcomes after combined TAA. Thirteen ankles that underwent combined TAA for end-stage varus ankle osteoarthritis were retrospectively evaluated. CT was performed preoperatively and 3 months postoperatively with the ankle in active dorsiflexion and plantarflexion under nonweightbearing. Preoperative and postoperative tibial models were registered using a globally optimal iterative closest point algorithm, enabling direct comparison of tibiotalar kinematics within a common tibial coordinate system. Spearman rank correlation was used to assess associations among preoperative kinematics, postoperative kinematics, longitudinal changes, and 2-year postoperative Self-Administered Foot Evaluation Questionnaire (SAFE-Q) scores. All SAFE-Q subscale scores improved significantly (P < .05 for all) after surgery. Postoperatively, inversion decreased and the rotational pattern between the 2 end positions shifted from external to internal rotation. Postoperative inversion correction, preservation of a physiological internal rotational relationship between the talus and tibia, and plantarflexion-related kinematic parameters showed associations with postoperative SAFE-Q scores. Greater longitudinal correction of plantarflexion inversion and dorsiflexion internal rotation was associated with superior postoperative pain-related outcomes. CT-based tibiotalar kinematics at maximum active dorsiflexion and plantarflexion showed exploratory associations with postoperative patient-reported outcomes after combined TAA. Restoration of postoperative inversion alignment, physiological internal rotational motion, and plantarflexion-related dynamic motion were associated with superior clinical outcomes. Given the small sample size, these findings should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating and require confirmation in larger cohorts. CT-based tibiotalar kinematics assessment using a common tibial coordinate system may provide a basis for further investigation of the relationship between postoperative tibiotalar kinematics and patient-reported outcomes after combined TAA. Level III, retrospective cohort study.

entry.title: Evaluating effects of a new hip-knee-ankle-foot orthosis on gait parameters in healthy individuals.
entry.content:
Barati K, Bidari S, Hadadi M, Karimi M, et al. · J Rehabil Assist Technol Eng · 2026

Hip-knee-ankle-foot orthoses (HKAFOs) are commonly used to assist gait; however, conventional designs are associated with high energy expenditure and poor mediolateral balance. This pilot study examined whether permitting additional motion in selected hip and ankle planes altered joint kinematics and dynamic-balance parameters in healthy participants. A randomized cross-over trial was conducted with 20 healthy participants aged 18-25. Gait performance was evaluated under five conditions: conventional HKAFO (locked/unlocked knee), Multiflex HKAFO (locked/unlocked knee), and no orthosis. Kinematic and balance data were collected. Key variables analyzed included center of pressure (CoP) velocity, mediolateral sway, and joint range of motion (ROM). Compared with the conventional HKAFO configurations, the Multiflex HKAFO permitted greater abduction/adduction and ankle inversion/eversion ROM. With the Multiflex HKAFO and an unlocked knee joint, CoP velocity and mediolateral excursion were not significantly different from walking without an orthosis. However, knee flexion/extension and ankle dorsiflexion/plantarflexion remained restricted relative to walking without an orthosis. In healthy participants, the Multiflex HKAFO permitted greater motion in selected hip and ankle planes than the conventional design while producing lower center-of-pressure velocity and mediolateral excursion in some configurations.

entry.title: Musical Feedback to Reduce the Knee Adduction Moment Via Center of Pressure Medialization: A Proof-of-Concept Study in Healthy Adults for Knee Osteoarthritis Gait Retraining.
entry.content:
Cedin L, Antognini C, Knowlton C, Ferrigno C, et al. · J Biomech · 2026

Elevated knee adduction moment (KAM) is a primary contributor to medial knee osteoarthritis (OA) progression. Medialization of center of pressure (CoP) can reduce KAM, but sustaining engagement and a consistent walking pattern remains a challenge. We investigated whether concurrent plantar pressure-modulated musical feedback would cue a medial CoP shift to reduce KAM without producing detrimental lower limb compensations in healthy adults. Twelve participants (6F/6M; age: 31.5 ± 5.3 years) walked while a marker-based motion analysis system (Qualisys) and wireless pressure-sensing insoles (Moticon) recorded gait. Real-time insole data drove auditory feedback: self-selected music was progressively muffled whenever the participant failed to shift their CoP medially beyond their threshold (25 % reduction in peak lateral CoP from baseline). Gait was assessed at baseline, post-instructions, and post-training. Repeated-measures ANOVA was used for kinetics and spatiotemporal outcomes, and statistical parametric mapping, as a secondary analysis, for kinematic waveforms. All participants medialized their CoP based on instructions and musical feedback. Musical feedback significantly reduced the second KAM peak (post-training: -13.7 %; p = 0.002) and the knee adduction angular impulse (post-training: -9.4 %; p < 0.001), but with a borderline increase in peak knee flexion moment (p = 0.050) that may reflect compensation. Gait adaptations were executed without a change in walking speed. Also, foot progression angle and stride width remained unchanged. CoP medialization was achieved mainly through ankle inversion, ankle external rotation, and hip internal rotation. These preliminary findings support concurrent sonified biofeedback for gait retraining, warranting evaluation in medial knee OA patients.

entry.title: Acute Responses in Dynamic Balance, Vertical Jump Performance, and Visuomotor Reaction Time Following Ankle Kinesio Taping and Dynamic Taping in Competitive Basketball Players: A Within-Subject Study.
entry.content:
Burma K, Kaya M, Demircioglu G · J Clin Med · 2026

Background/Objectives: Kinesio taping (KT) and dynamic taping (DT) are commonly used in sports settings to support sensorimotor function and athletic performance. However, evidence directly comparing their immediate effects across different performance domains in competitive basketball players remains limited. This study aimed to compare the acute responses to KT and DT in dynamic balance, vertical jump performance, and visuomotor reaction time. Methods: Twenty male competitive basketball players participated in this within-subject study. All participants received KT during the first testing session and DT during the second session conducted one week later. Dynamic balance, vertical jump performance, and visuomotor reaction time were assessed immediately before and after each taping application using the Lower Quarter Y-Balance Test, My Jump 2, and the Light Trainer system, respectively. Within-condition pre-post changes and differences in change between KT and DT were analyzed using paired-samples t-tests, with the Holm procedure applied to secondary outcomes to account for multiple comparisons. Results: Significant pre-post increases were observed in anterior and posterolateral reach and composite Y-Balance scores following both KT and DT (all p < 0.001). Posteromedial reach increased significantly following DT (p = 0.003) but not KT (p = 0.076), although the between-condition difference in change was not significant. Vertical jump performance and visuomotor reaction time showed no significant pre-post changes following either taping condition. No statistically significant between-condition differences were observed for any outcome. Conclusions: Both KT and DT were followed by immediate improvements in dynamic balance, whereas no statistically significant changes were detected in vertical jump performance or visuomotor reaction time. No statistically significant difference in the magnitude of change was observed between the two taping conditions. The differing response patterns across outcomes may indicate task-dependent acute responses; however, this interpretation should be considered preliminary given the study design and sample size.

entry.title: Effects of exercise-induced fatigue and lunge direction on racket-side lower-limb biomechanics during forward lunges in male badminton athletes.
entry.content:
Xie Z, Feng Z, Qiu Y, Jin Z, et al. · Front Bioeng Biotechnol · 2026

This study examined the effects of exercise-induced fatigue and lunge direction on racket-side lower-limb biomechanics during forehand and backhand forward lunges in male badminton athletes. Twenty-four male athletes performed standardized three-step lunges before and after a combined sprint-interval running and maximal vertical-jump fatigue protocol. Three-dimensional kinematics were recorded using a Vicon motion-capture system, while ground reaction forces were recorded using force platforms. Lower-limb biomechanical analyses focused on the racket-side limb. Outcome variables included phase durations, joint kinematics and moments, center-of-mass (COM) velocity, ground reaction forces (GRFs), impulses, joint quasi-stiffness, and dynamic postural stability. Outcomes were analyzed using two-way repeated-measures ANOVA with prespecified biomechanical-domain- and effect-specific Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction. No statistically significant fatigue × direction interactions were detected after BH correction; however, given the limited statistical sensitivity for interaction effects, these findings should be considered inconclusive. Fatigue shortened braking duration, reduced recovery-phase COM velocity gain, braking-phase impulses, recovery-phase anteroposterior impulse, and selected joint ROMs, while increasing recovery-phase hip and knee quasi-stiffness. Backhand lunges showed greater secondary-impact GRF, higher DPSI, VSI and MLSI values, greater ankle dorsiflexion and inversion, and a greater knee extension moment than forehand lunges. Within the racket-side limb, fatigue induced a more constrained lunge strategy and reduced recovery-phase impulse generation and COM velocity increase. Backhand lunges showed greater impact loading, braking-phase force fluctuations, and ankle mechanical demands than forehand lunges.

entry.title: Effects of chronic ankle instability on ipsilateral knee cartilage degeneration in mouse model.
entry.content:
Chen Z, Xu F, Chen B, Wang Z, et al. · Front Med Technol · 2026

To explore the effects of chronic ankle instability (CAI) on ipsilateral knee cartilage degeneration and the coupling relationship between the two joints through mouse model. Thirty C57BL/6J mice were divided into the Sham group, the CAI group, and the destabilization of medial meniscus (DMM) group. They were respectively subjected to sham surgery, anterior talofibular ligament and calcaneofibular ligament transection, and medial meniscus resection. The degeneration of knee cartilage was evaluated through kinematic experiments, imaging examinations and histopathological analysis within 12 weeks post-operation. The kinematic experiments exhibited significantly increased passing time and number of slips for CAI group compared to DMM group and Sham group during crossing the balance beam; the step length and step width of CAI group were also larger. Imaging examination revealed obvious osteochondral defects and osteosclerosis of the femoral condyles both in CAI group and DMM group at 12 weeks post-operation. However, the DMM group was more severely affected than CAI group, as its bone mineral density and bone volume fraction were both higher than CAI group. Histopathological analysis exhibited thinner cartilage layer, less chondrocytes and more disordered collagen fibers in DMM group than CAI group at 6 and 12 weeks post-operation. The modified Mankin score and OARSI score of DMM group were also significantly higher than CAI group, while both groups were higher than Sham group. CAI can cause cartilage degeneration of ipsilateral knee joint in mouse model, there is a coupling relationship between ankle joint and knee joint.

entry.title: Ankle Foot Orthosis Intervention Improves the Ground Reaction Forces During Walking in Patients with Peripheral Artery Disease (Randomized Clinical Trial).
entry.content:
Salamifar Z, Fallahtafti F, Samson K, Pipinos II, et al. · Actuators · 2026

This study investigated the impact of walking with ankle-foot-orthoses (AFOs) and without AFOs (non-AFO) on ground reaction forces (GRFs) in patients with peripheral artery disease (PAD). Additionally, this study examined the effect of AFO intervention vs. no AFO intervention on GRFs while walking with and without AFOs. Fifty patients with PAD were randomly assigned to either a three-month intervention (AFO) or a control (standard-of-care) group. After three months, subjects crossed over to the alternate group and were evaluated after three additional months. GRF data (anterior-posterior, medial-lateral, and vertical) were collected during walking with and without AFOs at baseline, three, and six months. Peak discrete GRF points, braking and propulsion impulses were compared across conditions, groups, and time points using linear mixed models. The peak brake and propulsion GRF were significantly reduced while walking with AFOs versus non-AFO (p < 0.01). Compared to non-AFO, walking with AFOs significantly reduced lateral GRF magnitude (p = 0.03) and significantly increased medial GRF (p = 0.02). The first and second maximum (p < 0.01) vertical GRF were significantly increased with AFOs versus non-AFOs. Walking with AFOs helped patients with PAD achieve greater peak propulsion and vertical GRFs compared to non-AFO, with GRF values trending toward those previously reported in healthy individuals.

entry.title: How Effectively Does Protective Sports Gear Prevent Sports Injuries?
entry.content:
Jami M, Mujadzic T, Marcelli AL, Netscher DTJ · South Med J · 2026

As organized and recreational sports continue to grow in popularity, associated sports injuries increasingly burden athletes. Protective sports gear is intended to reduce injury risk during play. This article provides a comprehensive review of the mechanism and efficacy of protective sports gear in injury prevention to the head and neck, upper extremity, and lower extremity and assesses where perhaps evidence for protection is lacking. Helmets, face shields, and protective eyewear have clear benefits in structural protection against injury. The impact of sports gear in reducing sport-related concussion is more variable, largely due to the repetitive nature of the injury mechanism where cumulative low-magnitude impacts contribute to brain injury. For the upper extremity, wrist guards have a clear benefit in reducing major and minor injuries among gymnasts and snowboarders and hence by inference on other impact sports. Ankle braces and taping potentially reduce the risk of ankle sprains among athletes, and the mandating of shin guards in professional soccer results in decreased sports-related lower extremity fractures. Further research is warranted to evaluate the effectiveness of sports gear on reinjury prevention and to study the implications of sports gear on risk compensation theory in athletes.

entry.title: Feedforward neuromuscular control and dynamic postural stability in people with chronic ankle instability during single-leg landing.
entry.content:
Li TY, Wang Z, Cascoe R, Aki-Sawyerr J, et al. · J Biomech · 2026

Individuals with chronic ankle instability(CAI) show deficits in neuromuscular control and postural stability. While feedback mechanisms are well-studied, feedforward mechanisms during dynamic tasks remains underexplored. This study compared feedforward neuromuscular control and dynamic postural stability among CAI, coper and healthy groups. Fifteen CAI(23.5 ± 2.9 years, 11 M/4F), fifteen coper(24.1 ± 3.4 years, 12 M/3F) and fifteen healthy participants(25.5 ± 3.5 years, 11 M/4F) performed single-leg drop landings from 30 cm. Total centre of pressure movement during 1-second and 3-second(TOTEX1s&TOTEX3s), mediolateral sway distance(DML), peak vertical GRF(peak vGRF) and root-mean-square of mediolateral GRF in the first 0.4 s(RMS_ML_0.4) were recorded via force plate. Surface electromyography recorded muscle activity 200 ms before landing among tibialis anterior(TA), peroneus longus(PL) and gastrocnemius lateralis(GL). Pre-activation timing was calculated using the Teager-Kaiser energy operator(TKEO). Statistical analysis involved one-way ANOVA(α = 0.05) and Tukey post-hoc testing. Compared to healthy participants, CAI individuals displayed earlier TA(270 ± 73 ms vs. 85 ± 53 ms, p < 0.001) and PL(260 ± 87 ms vs. 102 ± 62 ms, p < 0.001) pre-activations, alongside higher TA activity(76 ± 27% vs. 35 ± 19%, p < 0.001) but lower PL activity(38 ± 14% vs. 77 ± 23%, p < 0.001). Higher RMS_ML_0.4(6.7 ± 1.3%BW vs. 5.6 ± 1.0%BW, p = 0.037), DML(55.6 ± 15.7 mm vs. 39.5 ± 9.0 mm, p < 0.001) and peak vGRF(334 ± 44%BW vs. 286 ± 59%BW, p = 0.041)were observed as well. Coper showed earlier GL pre-activation(169 ± 57 ms vs. 108 ± 67 ms, p = 0.021), increased activity(155 ± 40% vs. 97 ± 29%, p < 0.001) and decreased DML(42.7 ± 7.0 mm vs. 55.6 ± 15.7 mm, p = 0.008) compared to CAI individuals. CAI exhibited postural control deficits and ineffective feedforward control, shown by lower PL activity despite early pre-activation. Rate of force production training is advised. Increased GL activation may serve as a compensatory response in copers after initial ankle sprain.

entry.title: [Sensorimotor insoles for musculoskeletal disorders : An evidence-based rapid review].
entry.content:
Walther M, Greitemann B, Kerkoff A, Seeßle M, et al. · Orthopadie (Heidelb) · 2026

Sensorimotor foot orthoses (SMFOs) are designed to modulate afferent input through targeted plantar stimuli and thereby influence neuromuscular control mechanisms. This review aimed to provide an evidence-based assessment of their clinical effectiveness across different musculoskeletal conditions. We conducted a rapid review of randomized controlled trials and systematic reviews. We evaluated the available evidence for different orthotic concepts on an indication-specific basis using the GRADE approach. The strongest evidence was for symptomatic flexible pes planovalgus and patellofemoral pain syndrome, although no consistent superiority of SMFOs over conventional supportive foot orthoses was demonstrated. In patients with patellofemoral pain syndrome, randomized data showed significant improvements in pain and function with both SMFOs and conventional foot orthoses. For chronic ankle instability, the evidence regarding sensorimotor interventions is largely limited to mechanistic and indirect outcomes. Interpretation is further complicated because the textured insoles used in many studies do not match what is traditionally understood as SMFOs in German-speaking orthopedic practice. Evidence for SMFOs in nonspecific low back pain is even more limited and is characterized by heterogeneous findings. Based on the current literature, no clear superiority of sensorimotor orthotic concepts can be demonstrated for any specific diagnosis. However, this should not be interpreted as evidence of general ineffectiveness. SMFOs represent a therapeutic option within multimodal treatment strategies and should be prescribed according to the individual indication and patient-specific treatment goals.

entry.title: Effects of sensorimotor training combined with short foot exercise on knee and ankle gait kinematics in individuals with flatfoot: A preliminary study.
entry.content:
Moon DC, Jung JH · Medicine (Baltimore) · 2026

Flatfoot, a common condition characterized by medial longitudinal arch collapse, alters foot and lower-limb mechanics. Sensorimotor training and short-foot exercises can improve postural stability and functional performance. However, their combined effects on gait kinematics remain unclear. This preliminary study evaluated the 6-week effects of combining these interventions on knee and ankle gait kinematics in individuals with flexible flatfeet. Thirty-two asymptomatic young adults with flexible flatfoot (14 males, 18 females; navicular drop ≥ 10 mm) were randomly assigned to an experimental group (sensorimotor training combined with short-foot exercises; n = 16) or a control group (sensorimotor training only; n = 16) using sealed opaque envelopes. Training was conducted 3 times per week for 6 weeks in a motion laboratory. Gait kinematics were assessed pre- and post-intervention using the VICON motion system. Outcomes included peak ankle inversion, eversion, dorsiflexion, and plantarflexion angles, knee internal and external rotation angles, and range of motion (ROM) in the sagittal, frontal, and transverse planes. Two-way repeated-measures analysis of variance was used for the analysis. The partial eta squared (ηp2) was reported as the effect size. Baseline demographics (age, sex, and body mass index) were similar between groups (P > .05). Significant group × time interactions were observed for gait variables. The experimental group showed a significant increase in peak ankle inversion (95% confidence interval (CI): 0.53-2.71; P = .004; ηp2 = 0.244) and a decrease in peak eversion (95% CI: 1.68-4.89; P = .002; ηp2 = 0.279). Peak knee internal rotation significantly decreased (95% CI: -9.92 to -2.82; P = .006; ηp2 = 0.228). Reductions were also observed in sagittal plane ankle ROM (95% CI: -4.88 to -0.68; P = .001; ηp2 = 0.317) and transverse plane knee ROM (95% CI: -7.75 to -4.01; P = .003; ηp2 = 0.254). No significant changes were found in ankle dorsiflexion, plantarflexion, knee external rotation, or frontal plane ankle ROM (P = .088, .126, .766, .136, respectively; ηp2 = 0.003-0.094). Combined sensorimotor and short-foot training more effectively improved gait kinematics than sensorimotor training alone, suggesting a promising non-surgical approach for managing flatfoot.

entry.title: Ankle Proprioceptive Performance on Increasingly Challenging Functional Tasks in Groups With and Without Chronic Ankle Instability.
entry.content:
Wang X, Shao X, Shi X, Adams RD, et al. · J Sport Rehabil · 2026

Up to 75% of lateral ankle sprain cases experience long-term impairments and suffer chronic ankle instability (CAI), a condition characterized by impaired ankle proprioception. This study aims to investigate ankle proprioceptive performance during functional tasks with increasing movement control and ankle joint load in individuals with and without CAI. Cross-sectional study. Twenty individuals with CAI and 19 healthy controls completed 4 proprioceptive tasks: standing, walking, landing (double-leg drop), and stair descent. In each task, their ability to discriminate between 4 ankle inversion angles was assessed using a task-specific discrimination apparatus. CAI participants had significantly lower ankle proprioception scores than controls (mean difference = 0.047, 95% CI, 0.031-0.063). Proprioceptive acuity varied by task (P < .001, ηp2=.345), with no significant group-by-task interaction (P = .220, ηp2=.039). Trend analysis showed a linear improvement in proprioceptive performance with increasing ankle load and challenge in controls (P < .001, ηp2=.685), whereas the CAI group showed both significant linear (P < .001, ηp2=.445) and quadratic (P = .001, ηp2=.430) trends, reflecting a rise followed by a significant downturn as load peaked. Both groups improved with greater load, but during stair descent, individuals with CAI exhibited a significant decline. This suggests that proprioceptive processing in CAI is impaired and may be overloaded during highly challenging tasks.

entry.title: Gait speed and multi-segment foot joint kinematics throughout the entire stance phase using statistical parametric mapping.
entry.content:
Jeong H, Hamill J, Boyer KA, van Emmerik REA · PeerJ · 2026

The foot is a multi-segment structure whose segments function together. Due to its ongoing connection with the support surface, the foot must be capable of managing loads that vary with gait speed. Previous studies have provided considerable insight into the relationship between foot joint kinematics and gait speed. However, their primary reliance on discrete measures, such as peak joint angles, has limited understanding of how these relationships evolve throughout the stance phase. The aim of this study was to investigate the effects of gait speed on full time-series trajectories of multiplanar foot joint kinematics using statistical parametric mapping. According to our findings, faster walking primarily increased ankle eversion and midfoot dorsiflexion during weight acceptance (∼17-29% of the stance phase). In contrast, during propulsion, faster walking increased ankle plantar flexion (∼80-100% of the stance phase) and inversion (∼82-90%), as well as midfoot plantar flexion (∼82-100%) and adduction (∼90-98%), together with greater dorsiflexion of the first metatarsophalangeal joint after heel-off (∼43-98% of the stance phase). These multiplanar joint kinematic alterations across the ankle-foot joints throughout the stance phase reflect greater foot-arch collapse in early stance and foot-arch recoil in late stance, which may facilitate appropriate energy absorption and generation in response to increasing gait speed. Importantly, these adaptive foot motions were not captured by previous discrete analyses, which may obscure phase-dependent changes during gait. The present continuous time-series approach revealed detailed temporal adaptations in foot kinematics across the stance phase, providing a more comprehensive characterization of gait mechanics.

entry.title: Using Wearable Sensors and Video Analysis to Improve Functional Electrical Stimulation Prescription in Individuals With Multiple Sclerosis: A Case Series.
entry.content:
Jackson K, Hosseini S, Bigelow K · Int J MS Care · 2026

A growing body of evidence supports the use of functional electrical stimulation (FES) in people with multiple sclerosis (MS). However, prescription remains an imprecise process with no well-established guidelines for assessing the immediate or long-term effects to ensure maximum benefit. The purpose of this case series was to assess the potential benefits of using wearable sensors and video analysis to provide immediate feedback on gait performance to improve FES prescription in people with MS. Three adults (2 women, 1 man; age range, 39-62 years) with MS with varying levels of lower extremity motor function and gait impairment were enrolled. During a single visit, participants performed a series of 10-m walks under various FES and non-FES conditions while using wearable motion sensors. Additionally, 2D video analysis was used to assess alterations in knee angles during swing and stance phases. All participants demonstrated improvements in a variety of gait variables, including a clinically meaningful (> 0.1 m/s) increase in gait speed during 1 or more of the FES conditions when compared with the no-device and/or prescribed ankle foot orthosis conditions. There were additional improvements associated with multichannel stimulation of the lower leg and thigh for certain gait variables. Data from the wearable sensors and video analysis were advantageous in helping researchers determine the most appropriate FES prescription for each participant. This case series demonstrates the potential clinical usefulness of these technologies in prescribing FES for people with MS.

entry.title: [Posttraumatic ankle arthrofibrosis : Diagnosis, prevention and treatment].
entry.content:
Al-Qaysi B, Winter P, Landgraeber S, Wagener J, et al. · Unfallchirurgie (Heidelb) · 2026

Posttraumatic arthrofibrosis is a rare cause of painful motion loss after injury or surgery, with limited available evidence. Posttraumatic arthrofibrosis is characterized by painful, progressive stiffness with more than 30% loss of motion and no major radiographic abnormality. Reported rates range from 2% to 10% after ankle injuries to up to 73% after surgically treated fractures, while ankle-specific data on risk factors remain limited. The pathogenesis appears to involve transforming growth factor (TGF)-β, interleukin (IL)-1, and hypoxia-mediated capsular fibrosis. Arthrography remains the diagnostic gold standard according to the Goldman criteria. Magnetic resonance imaging may show capsular thickening ≥ 3 mm and stage-dependent signal changes. First-line treatment comprises physiotherapy, mobilization, and dynamic or static progressive orthoses. A mean 17° gain in total range of motion was reported with static progressive orthoses. In refractory stiffness, arthroscopic capsular release may be beneficial, with improvement of the American Orthopaedic Foot and Ankle Society (AOFAS) score from 63.8 to 88.6, dorsiflexion from 1 to 19°, and acceptable motion in more than 80% of patients. Posttraumatic arthrofibrosis of the ankle is rare, underdiagnosed, and treatable. Early recognition and stepwise conservative treatment, followed by arthroscopic capsular release, may restore function. The evidence is based mainly on small level IV studies. Prospective studies are required.

entry.title: Auditory Biofeedback Gait Training in Individuals With Chronic Ankle Instability: Protocol for a Randomized Controlled Trial.
entry.content:
Torp DM, Choi JY, Edison A, Hoch M, et al. · JMIR Res Protoc · 2026

Chronic ankle instability (CAI) develops in a large majority of patients with lateral ankle sprain (LAS), who often experience recurring injuries, residual feelings of instability, and abnormal neuromuscular patterns. Specifically, gait alterations are common in those with CAI and considered a contributing factor to poor long-term ankle joint health. Yet, there are no evidence-based gait-training protocols targeted to improve biomechanics, which may improve long-term outcomes related to ankle joint health and patient satisfaction. This study protocol introduces a progressive auditory biofeedback (ABF) gait-training program aimed to improve short- and long-term lower extremity biomechanics and talar cartilage outcomes and reduce the frequency of ankle-giving-way episodes and recurring injuries. This study is a multisite randomized controlled trial (RCT) with a target enrollment of 100 patients with CAI into a control group (n=50, 50%) or an ABF gait-training program (n=50, 50%). Both groups will complete a progressive 6-week (12-session) protocol comprising walking, ruck marching, and running on a treadmill. Lower extremity kinematics and kinetics, talar cartilage characteristics (via ultrasonography), self-perceived dysfunction and instability, and number of recurring sprains will be assessed prior to intervention, immediately after intervention, and 6 and 12 months postintervention. Finally, the frequency of ankle-giving-way episodes in the 6 months prior to intervention will be compared to the frequency of episodes at the 6- and 12-month time points to determine a longitudinal difference in ankle-giving-way episodes. The study was funded in September 2024 and prospectively registered through ClinicalTrials.gov on March 10, 2025. The first participant was enrolled in May 2025. As of August 2026, 118 individuals had been recruited and 19 participants enrolled. Recruitment will remain open until September 2027, and study completion is expected in September 2028. Data processing is projected to continue through September 2028, with the final report published in June 2029. This study will be the first RCT of ABF gait training to assess the immediate and long-term effects on lower extremity biomechanics, ankle joint health, and patient-reported outcomes in patients with CAI. Results from this study will advance the knowledge of long-term joint health that may be associated with poor outcomes post-LAS. entry.title: Pain-stratified differences in lower-limb mechanics and neuromuscular activation during single-leg drop landing in male athletes with chronic ankle instability.
entry.content:
Wang Z, Zheng W, Zhou Z, Wang X · Phys Ther Sport · 2026

To compare mechanical and neuromuscular strategies between high- and low-pain subgroups of male athletes with chronic ankle instability (CAI) during single-leg drop landing. Cross-sectional study. Biomechanics laboratory. Eighty-four male Tier 2-3 athletes, stratified into high-pain CAI (n = 28), low-pain CAI (n = 28), and healthy control (n = 28) groups. Lower-limb kinematics, impact loading, joint moments, eccentric work and energy contributions, surface electromyographic root mean square amplitude, and co-contraction index. Significant group effects were observed for kinematic outcomes (p ≤ 0.042; ηp2 = 0.075-0.384), joint kinetics and energetics (p ≤ 0.042; ηp2 = 0.075-0.561), and neuromuscular outcomes (p = 0.005-0.017; ηp2 = 0.096-0.124). The high-pain CAI group exhibited lower ankle plantarflexor moment than both comparison groups (both p < 0.001; d = 1.192-1.210), lower ankle eccentric work (p ≤ 0.001; d = 1.030-1.853), lower ankle energy contribution (p ≤ 0.002; d = 0.983-2.133), and greater knee energy contribution (both p < 0.001; d = 1.209-1.818). The low-pain CAI group exhibited less hip flexion and greater ankle plantarflexion at initial contact and greater ankle dorsiflexion range of motion (p ≤ 0.024; d = 0.736-1.398). The high-pain CAI group showed greater tibialis anterior activation than the low-pain group (p = 0.004; d = 0.903) and greater rectus femoris-biceps femoris co-contraction than controls (p = 0.045; d = 0.672). External impact-loading measures did not differ among groups (p = 0.114-0.265; ηp2 = 0.032-0.058). Pain-defined CAI subgroups differed in interjoint load sharing and selected neuromuscular measures despite comparable external impact loading.

entry.title: Association of Ankle Joint Moment and Ankle Joint Velocity With 60° Ipsilateral Change-of-Direction Performance.
entry.content:
Chen CH, Yeh M, Liu C, Tseng YJ, et al. · J Strength Cond Res · 2026

Chen, C-H, Yeh, M-C, Liu, C, Tseng, Y-J, and Lu, S-T. Association of ankle joint moment and ankle joint velocity with 60° ipsilateral change-of-direction performance. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The rapid acceleration and deceleration associated with a change of direction (COD) is associated with high ankle loading, including high ankle moment and velocity, which have been linked to ankle sprain or chronic ankle instability. Although the correlations between ankle joint loading and contralateral COD (contra-COD) have been investigated, one study reported that ipsilateral COD (ipsi-COD) and contra-COD involve distinct, asymmetrical mechanisms. Therefore, the aim of this study is to evaluate the associations of ankle joint moment and ankle joint velocity with 60° ipsi-COD performance. Thirty-five male athletes of recreational team sports performed an ipsi-COD task with their nondominant leg. A three-dimensional motion-capture system and a force platform were used to collect biomechanical data. Ground contact time was negatively associated with plantarflexion moment (r = -0.511) and inversion moment (r = -0.424). By contrast, horizontal impulse was positively correlated with plantarflexion moment (r = 0.407). No correlation was observed between ground contact time and ground reaction force. The moderate negative correlations of ground contact time with plantarflexion moment and inversion moment suggest that increasing ipsi-COD performance may result in high ankle moments and potentially excessive ankle loading. In addition, the absence of a correlation between ground contact time and GRF suggests that athletes consider focusing on converting their approaching velocity to the intended direction during ipsi-COD, as this study indicates that ground reaction force and impulse are not associated with ipsi-COD performance.

entry.title: Side-Step Cutting Foot Biomechanics and Intrinsic Foot Muscle Sizes in People With Chronic Ankle Instability.
entry.content:
Peters-Dickie JL, Detrembleur C, Lobet S, Deschamps K · J Foot Ankle Res · 2026

Lateral ankle sprains commonly occur during directional changes and often lead to chronic ankle instability (CAI) associated with altered movement patterns, muscle weakness and atrophy. This study aimed to compare foot joint biomechanics during cutting among individuals with CAI, copers, and uninjured controls and to explore the relationship between intrinsic foot muscle sizes and functional status. Cross-sectional study. Sixty-nine recreationally active males (25.4 ± 4 years) were categorised by perceived instability and self-reported function. Ankle and foot joint kinematics and kinetics were assessed using a multi-segment foot model during 45° side-step cutting at a mean approach speed of 3.5 m·s-1. Groups were compared using ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis tests, and continuous biomechanical data were analysed using statistical parametric or non-parametric mapping. Cross-sectional area and thickness of the abductor hallucis and flexor digitorum brevis were recorded using ultrasound imaging. Muscle sizes were explored using general linear models, and correlations with questionnaire scores and physical examination outcomes were calculated. Foot joint kinematics and kinetics did not significantly differ between the groups. Individuals with CAI exhibited lower peak posterior ground reaction force than controls (mean difference: -6.2% of body weight, 95% CI: -11.9 to -0.4, p = 0.03). Statistical parametric mapping revealed lower posterior ground reaction forces from 22% to 46% of stance in CAI versus controls (p < 0.05). Intrinsic foot muscle sizes showed weak, statistically significant negative correlations with perceived instability scores (ρ = -0.31 to -0.36) and self-reported function scores (ρ = -0.26 to -0.33). Despite pronounced sensory-perceptual impairments, individuals with CAI demonstrated few differences in foot joint biomechanics compared with copers and controls during a moderate-speed anticipated cutting task. Reduced braking forces may reflect altered deceleration strategies. These findings suggest the importance of assessing deceleration abilities in people with CAI and indicate a potential role of foot muscles in CAI-related functional outcomes. entry.title: Feedforward Pre-Activation of Lateral Ankle Muscles Is Insufficient Against Excessive Ankle Inversion During Perturbation in Individuals With Chronic Ankle Instability.
entry.content:
Ran W, Song Q, Yin W · J Foot Ankle Res · 2026

This study aimed to compare ankle kinematics and muscle activation between individuals with and without chronic ankle instability (CAI), both prior to and following landing on an inversion trapdoor during walking, with a particular focus on the feedforward pre-activation of lateral ankle muscles and the consequent ankle kinematics post-perturbation. Forty participants were enrolled, including 20 with CAI and 20 age- and sex-matched non-CAI controls. They walked at their own pace on a custom-designed walking platform equipped with a trapdoor programmed to trigger a 24° inversion perturbation, simulating lateral ankle sprain conditions, across three unanticipated trials. Their lower limb muscle electromyography and ankle kinematics were synchronously collected 200 ms pre- and 200 ms post-perturbation. Continuous between-group data were compared by independent sample t-tests. CAI individuals showed higher pre-activation in the peroneus longus (-200.0 to -196.4 ms, mean diff: -11.38%, p = 0.049; -54.6 to -11.0 ms, mean diff: -10.60%, p = 0.011) and the lateral gastrocnemius (-200.0 to -175.4 ms, mean diff: -7.62%, p = 0.029) prior to perturbation, and lower activation in the peroneus longus at 72.1 to 98.0 ms (mean diff: 17.46%, p = 0.029) post-perturbation. They also showed greater ankle inversion in four clusters post-perturbation (0 to 111.0 ms, mean diff: -4.85°, p < 0.001; 117.0 to 128.0 ms, mean diff: -1.83°, p = 0.020; 142.0 to 145.0 ms, mean diff: -1.30°, p = 0.047; 154.0 to 165.0 ms, mean diff: -1.05°, p = 0.019). CAI individuals exhibit higher feedforward pre-activation in lateral ankle muscles, which may be insufficient against excessive ankle inversion after landing on a trapdoor during walking.
